entries.content:
Have you ever found yourself waking up feeling perfectly normal and then being told by your wearable app that you've slept poorly? And perhaps not only that, but somehow finding yourself starting to feel a bit tired just because of it? Well, yeah, me too.

As a wearables person, I'm definitely not going to recommend that you give up on your tracking device and put it into a drawer. But there are some things we should discuss about when a number starts being valued above your actual feelings and how you can use your smart device effectively.

What We'll Cover:

Morning Scores and How They Affect Your Day

Readiness scores and sleep scores are designed to be glanceable. This is their key advantage. The problem is that glancing leads to checking, which leads to checking becoming an uncontrollable addiction. You reach for your smartphone before you even drink your first glass of water in the morning and receive a judgement about your own body.

In case of a high score, you feel great. In case of a low score, you look for reasons why you don't feel great. Your legs are heavy? Sure, sounds right. Your throat feels scratchy? Yep, most likely. But you felt just great 5 minutes ago.

There are a lot of discussions about sensors, battery life, and titanium finish (I'm guilty of this, too). But people spend little to no time on discussing the experience of having your health grade updated daily.

It also impacts your behavior. People avoid working out when the app says their recovery level is low and other people train when the score is green even if they feel terrible. In any case, the app makes a decision for you that your body used to make.

Enter Orthosomnia

Sleep gave a name to this phenomenon. In 2017, researchers from Rush University and Northwestern described three patients in a case series in the Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine. The patients' sleep complaints came mostly from their tracker data. Stretches of light or restless sleep on the app had convinced them they had insomnia or weren't getting enough rest. The authors called it orthosomnia, or an obsession with "good" sleep (which is a nod to orthorexia, the unhealthy preoccupation with eating "correctly").

The part that really caught my attention is that one of the patients, a lady who had trouble feeling refreshed, believed her Fitbit over a lab study that demonstrated that she got plenty of deep sleep. It became quite difficult for anyone to convince her otherwise.

That being said, the study only focused on three cases so it's certainly not extensive. I won't go into too much hype about it. But if you've experienced seeing (and perhaps wincing at) your sleep score after waking up at 7 am, then you'll understand what I mean.

Obsessing About the Number Makes You Sleep Worse

There's one point from the write-up about Rush University researchers that I'll remember forever. The subjects of the study were basically increasing the amount of sleep shown by their trackers by spending more and more hours in bed. But this goes against the recommendation of sleep therapists. So a device which is meant to improve a person's sleep was encouraging them to develop habits which hinder good sleep.

Dr. Kelly Glazer Baron, the first author of the study, also mentioned that these devices can't differentiate between light and deep sleep and may treat even reading in bed as sleep. She also emphasized that such devices can't be used to diagnose sleep apnea.

How Accurate Is Your Dashboard?

This is a good question, because if all the data were perfectly measured, it wouldn't really matter. And in fact, wearables can actually deal with the basics pretty well. Distinguishing between asleep or awake periods and measuring their duration, for example. But estimating sleep stages is when they have a harder time: the classic deep, light, and REM classification we're all interested in.

A 2024 study in the journal Sensors compared the performance of Oura Ring Gen3, Fitbit Sense 2, and Apple Watch Series 8 to polysomnography (PSG), which is the laboratory method gold standard. The test was carried out using 35 healthy volunteers, aged 20 to 50 years, during one night.

The results were interesting. All three wearables produced total sleep duration estimates that were statistically similar to the PSG results. They also detected sleep periods with at least 95% sensitivity (more on sensitivity below). But their ability to identify individual sleep stages varied considerably.

For light, deep, and REM sleep, the sensitivity results were:

  • Oura Ring Gen 3: 78.2% for light sleep, 79.5% for deep sleep, and 76% for REM sleep.
  • Fitbit Sense 2: 78% for light sleep, 61.7% for deep sleep, and 67.3% for REM sleep.
  • Apple Watch Series 8: 86.1% for light sleep, 50.5% for deep sleep, and 82.6% for REM sleep.

These numbers tell us that even when a wearable can estimate how long you slept reasonably well, it may struggle to identify exactly which sleep stage you were in. For example, the Apple Watch identified only 50.5% of the deep-sleep periods recorded by PSG. That's quite a difference when we're talking about something as specific as sleep stages.

It's important to understand that sensitivity doesn't tell the whole story. It measures how often a device correctly identifies a particular sleep stage when PSG detects it, but it doesn't tell us how often the device's own sleep-stage predictions are correct. So these percentages are useful for understanding where wearables struggle, but they shouldn't be treated as an overall accuracy score.

There were also differences in the estimated duration of individual stages. Oura's estimates of wake, light, deep, and REM sleep were not significantly different from PSG. Fitbit overestimated light sleep by 18 minutes and underestimated deep sleep by 15 minutes. The Apple Watch underestimated deep sleep by 43 minutes and overestimated light sleep by 45 minutes.

As an Oura user myself, I find its sleep tracking useful, but these results show why I wouldn't treat every number as an exact measurement. The study suggests that wearables can be quite helpful in estimating overall sleep duration, while individual sleep-stage readings still have limitations. It's also worth remembering that this was a single-night study involving healthy sleepers, so we shouldn't assume the same results will apply to everyone or across different nights.

So, when your app tells you that you got 41 minutes of deep sleep, don't immediately assume that's exactly what happened. It's an estimate based on sensor data, not a laboratory measurement.

All this Goes Beyond Sleep

Sleep gets all the credit, but heart rate, HRV, stress numbers and step counts can do exactly the same thing to your mind.

In a 2020 study, researchers at the University of Copenhagen tracked 27 heart disease patients with arrhythmias or pacemakers for six months using Fitbits. They monitored sleep quality, heart rate, and physical activity.

Participants learned more about their health conditions and became motivated to exercise. But on the other hand, they became more anxious. Bad sleep numbers would frighten them and failing to achieve 10,000 steps per day made them feel guilty. Tariq Osman Andersen, one of the researchers, said that the overall effect of self-monitoring was "more problematic than beneficial."

This was a relatively small sample size with a certain health condition, so I don't want to generalize too much here about the overall benefits of sleep and fitness tracking. But the idea can apply to anyone. A concerning number without any additional information or context is easy to interpret as a danger signal.

When Helpful App Features Become a Source of Pressure

A 2024 systematic review published in the Journal of Public Policy & Marketing explored the negative effects of health and fitness technologies. The researchers reviewed 65 publications and found that 42 of them (64.6%) reported negative emotional outcomes associated with these technologies. Guilt, pressure, stress, anxiety, and frustration were among the most commonly reported feelings.

But what I find interesting here is that the problem isn't necessarily the tracking itself. Some of the features designed to keep people motivated can also become a source of pressure.

The review identified unmet goals and negative feedback as two particularly important examples. Failure to achieve goals was discussed in 23 publications, while negative feedback appeared in 15. Reminders and notifications were also linked to feelings of stress and annoyance.

Think about daily goals, for example. Your wearable encourages you to complete 10,000 steps, close your activity rings, or maintain a sleep schedule. These targets can be useful, but repeatedly failing to achieve them can leave you feeling guilty or disappointed.

The same goes for feedback. Notifications reminding you about missed goals or showing poor performance can make you feel as though you're falling behind, even when you're making reasonable progress.

Then there's the gamification aspect. Leaderboards, achievement badges, streaks and social competitions encourage people to stay active and keep using their devices. But they can also make users compare their performance with others. When someone consistently sees their friends taking more steps or achieving better results, it can create unnecessary pressure and frustration.

This doesn't mean these features are inherently bad or that everyone will experience these problems. The review found associations between certain app features and negative emotional experiences, rather than proving that these features directly cause them in every user.

It makes sense when you think about it. These applications are designed to encourage you to check your progress, achieve your goals, and keep improving. But sometimes, the constant reminders of what you haven't achieved can become more noticeable than the progress you have actually made.

Why Your Score Can Feel So Convincing

The number seems objective because it was read from the sensor and displayed on a neat app. In contrast, your own sense of being tired is vague and annoying, so the number becomes more believable even though it's not supposed to be so.

Also, the apps almost never inform you of the degree of uncertainty of the estimate. There's no small note saying that the result is an approximation with an error range. You only see "62" in red. Because the scores are yours, a low score is something very personal.

Things are even worse when you're already stressed out. If you're concerned about sleeping poorly, a poor score just proves it and can feel like it manifests it and you become stressed about the score as well.

The Jewelry Problem

This one is unique to the area I'm talking about. The whole idea of smart rings and good-looking watches is that you simply forget they're there. You wear them to the gym, to dinner, and to bed. That's some serious design there.

That also means that the monitoring never ends and the scoring continues as well. A cumbersome device that's removed before bed takes a rest automatically. Not so with a ring you forget about.

Where Tracking Genuinely Helps

I'm not trying to say that this data is pointless, since it isn't. Realizing that you have poor sleep from eating late dinners or traveling a lot can ruin your whole week, but it can be valid information. It can even help you realize that you've been living on five hours of sleep a day for a month, which might encourage you to make some changes. After all, these applications are great at picking up patterns.

This is where the problem lies: when you use the same application to assess one night's sleep or how you feel on one particular morning, that's not the best information. Patterns over time hold the most valuable data. One individual assessment is nothing more than noise.

What I'd Actually Do

I'm not anti-tracking. I just think you should set a few ground rules to help you use the app in a helpful way.

  • Look at weekly trends, not single nights. One bad score tells you almost nothing.
  • Check how you feel first, then open the app. If you feel fine, the score doesn't matter nearly as much.
  • Turn off notifications that nudge you about sleep or stress.
  • If a number makes you feel worse for a couple of weeks straight, take a break. A week without your ring is fine. See how you feel without it.
  • For real symptoms, see a doctor. Trackers can give you something to ask about, but they can't diagnose you.

Wrapping Up

The technology isn't necessarily the bad thing here. My study of the existing literature reveals that the problem arises when the number starts to overrule your personal experience and feelings. And we shouldn't forget that we're all able to track our own health and how we feel without these tools.

Still, wearables are great at detecting patterns and they're very good at basics. Just remember that anything else is just an educated guess.

So I encourage you to look at the numbers, take and use what's valuable to you, and move on with your life.

Put on the ring, appreciate the data, and every once in a while check in with yourself about how you actually feel rather than what the app suggests you should feel. If there's disagreement, I'd believe yourself over a device.

entries.title: How to Deploy to Amazon S3 Using GitLab CI/CD and AWS OIDC Without AWS Access Keys

entries.content:
When you're learning AWS, Amazon S3 is one of the services you're likely to come across early. Storage is one of the core components of cloud computing, and S3 makes it easy to store and manage files in the cloud.

If you've worked with S3 before, you probably know how to create a bucket and manually upload files through the AWS Management Console. But what happens when you need to deploy files regularly? Would you want to keep uploading them manually every time you make a change? This is where automation comes in.

In this tutorial, I'll show you how to automate the deployment of files to an Amazon S3 bucket using GitLab CI/CD. We'll also configure OpenID Connect (OIDC) to establish a secure connection between GitLab and AWS without storing long-lived AWS access keys in GitLab CI/CD variables.

By the end of this tutorial, you'll know how to configure a GitLab CI/CD pipeline, connect GitLab to AWS using OIDC, and automatically deploy files to an S3 bucket whenever you push changes to your GitLab repository.

Let's get started!

Table of Contents

Prerequisites

Before getting started, make sure you have the following:

  • A basic understanding of cloud computing and AWS.
  • An AWS account.
  • A GitLab account to store your code and automate deployment.
  • A code editor like VS Code, Atom, or Sublime

Note: I'll be using GitLab for this tutorial. If you use GitHub instead, you can also get the same result using GitHub Actions. Both platforms support automated deployment.

Before setting up Amazon S3 for automated deployment, let's take a step back and understand why this approach is worth learning.

You might be wondering, why should I automate file deployment? What are the advantages? These are valid questions, and understanding the answers will help you see where automation fits into your cloud workflow.

Let's look at them before moving on to the practical steps.

Why Should I Automate My Deployments?

Imagine your website is hosted on Amazon S3. Every time you make a change, you have to log in to the AWS Console, open your S3 bucket, and manually upload the new files.

That is fine for a small project that rarely changes. But what if you need to update your site often?

Uploading files by hand repeatedly gets boring and takes some time.

This is where automation helps. With GitLab CI/CD or GitHub Actions, you can set up a pipeline that sends your files to S3 for you. Every time you push changes to GitLab, the pipeline runs and deploys your site.

So instead of uploading files yourself, GitLab does it for you.

What Are the Advantages of This?

Using GitLab CI/CD to deploy files to Amazon S3 has several advantages:

  1. Faster deployment: Once the pipeline is set up, you just push your changes to GitLab, and the deployment starts on its own.
  2. Fewer mistakes: The pipeline follows the same steps every time, so you're less likely to forget a file or upload the wrong version.
  3. Less manual work: You don't have to repeat the upload process through the AWS Console whenever you update your files.
  4. Version control: Your website files live in GitLab, so you can track changes, look at old commits, and see what was updated.

What is CI/CD, and Why Does it Matter?

CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery or Continuous Deployment.

In simple terms, it's a way to automate the steps of testing and deploying your code, so you don’t have to do each step by hand. Think of it as giving a set of instructions to follow whenever you push changes to your repository.

In this tutorial, GitLab CI/CD will deploy your files to Amazon S3. When you push changes to your GitLab repository, GitLab starts a pipeline. The pipeline follows the steps you wrote in your 

.gitlab-ci.yml
file and uploads your updated files to your S3 bucket.

As I said earlier, CI/CD makes deployment easier, saves you from repeating the same work, and keeps your deployment process the same every time.

What is OpenID Connect (OIDC), and Why Use it?

We'll use OpenID Connect (OIDC) in this tutorial to connect GitLab to AWS safely. But what is OIDC, and why do we need it?

OIDC is a way for one service to prove who it is to another service. In our case, it lets GitLab prove its identity to AWS.

Without OIDC, you would have to save your AWS access keys in GitLab. These keys don't expire, so if someone gets hold of them, they can use your AWS account.

With OIDC, you don't save any keys. When your pipeline runs, GitLab proves its identity to AWS, and AWS gives it a temporary key. This key stops working after the job is done. This is safer, and you have no long-term keys to store or manage.

Advantages of Using OIDC

  • You don't need to store permanent AWS access keys in GitLab.
  • AWS provides credentials that expire after a set period.
  • OIDC reduces the risk of exposing long-term AWS credentials.

Are There Any Disadvantages?

The initial setup requires some additional configuration in AWS IAM and GitLab. You need to configure the identity provider, IAM role, and permissions before the connection can work.

But once it's configured, you can reuse this authentication setup for your deployment pipeline.

Now that you understand why we're using GitLab CI/CD and OIDC, let's move on to the practical part and set everything up.

Step 1: Prepare Your Website Files (Code) and Upload Them to GitLab

Before you can deploy your website to Amazon S3, you need to create the website files and upload them to your GitLab repository.

Open your preferred code editor, such as VS Code and create a new project folder named 

s3-website
.

Inside the folder, create two HTML files:

  • index.html
    : This will be the homepage visitors see when they open your website.
  • error.html
    : This will be displayed when a visitor encounters an error.

Write your HTML code in each file and save your changes.

Then open 

index.html
in your browser to check that the homepage displays correctly. Test 
error.html
to make sure it displays as expected.

Once you're satisfied with the files, open your GitLab repository and upload both HTML files to the repository. Then commit your changes to the 

main
branch.

Your GitLab repository should now contain:

practice-action-aws/
├── index.html
└── error.html

These are the files your GitLab CI/CD pipeline will automatically deploy to the S3 bucket.

Step 2: Create an Amazon S3 Bucket

The next step is to create an S3 bucket where GitLab will deploy your files.

To do this, sign in to the AWS Management Console, search for S3, and open the service. Click Create bucket.

Enter a unique name for your bucket. For example, 

gitlab-s3-deployment-demo-bucket
. You'll also need to select the AWS Region where you want to create the bucket. Remember the region because you'll need it later when configuring GitLab.

Step 3: Give Your S3 Bucket Public Access

Now that you've created your S3 bucket, the next step is to give it public access.

We're doing this for learning purposes here so we can demonstrate how publicly accessible files work. In a real-world production environment, you should avoid making your S3 bucket public unless there's a specific requirement and appropriate security controls are in place.

To give it public access, click on the bucket you created. Then click the Permissions tab at the top.

Locate Block public access (bucket settings) and click Edit. Uncheck Block all public access. AWS will display a warning. Read it, acknowledge the change, and click Save changes.

Next, scroll down to the bucket policy and click Edit. Paste the bucket policy below, replacing the existing content if necessary.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "PublicReadGetObject",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:GetObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::gitlab-s3-deployment-demo-bucket/*"
    }
  ]
}

Click Save changes.

The next step is to enable static website hosting. This is important because we don't just want to deploy files to S3 automatically. We want to make our website accessible through a browser.

Step 4: Enable Static Website Hosting

Now that you've configured public access, let's enable static website hosting for your S3 bucket.

To start, click on the Properties tab. Scroll down to the Static website hosting section and click Edit.

Under Static website hosting, select Enable. Then select Host a static website as the hosting type.

Under the Index document, enter 

index.html
. Same for the error field 
error.html
. Click Save changes.

Once saved, scroll back to the Static website hosting section. You should see your website endpoint.

This endpoint is the URL through which visitors can access your website.

Step 5: Configure AWS IAM for GitLab OIDC Authentication

Now that your S3 bucket is set up for static website hosting, the next step is to set up AWS IAM.

We need to permit GitLab to upload files to your S3 bucket whenever you push changes to your repository.

To do this, we'll use OIDC. It lets GitLab connect to AWS and get temporary credentials, so you don't have to save long-term AWS access keys in GitLab.

How to Create an OIDC Identity Provider in AWS

Search for IAM and open it. In the left menu, click Identity providers. Then click Add provider.

Select OpenID Connect as the provider type and enter these details:

FieldValue
Provider URL
https://gitlab.com
Audience
sts.amazonaws.com
  1. Click Add provider.

This tells AWS to trust GitLab as an identity provider. In the next step, you'll create an IAM role that uses it.

Step 6: Create an IAM Role for GitLab

Now that you've created the OIDC identity provider, you'll need to create an IAM role that GitLab can assume to access your S3 bucket.

This role will define what GitLab is allowed to do in your AWS account.

To start, click Roles in the left navigation panel or follow the on-screen banner, then click Create role.

  • Under Trusted entity type, select 
    Web identity
  • Under Identity Provider, select 
    gitlab.com
  • Under Audience, select 
    sts.amazonaws.com
  • Under Group type, in your 
    username

The other fields are optional.

Then click Next and Next. Finally, click the Create role button.

Step 7: Attach S3 Permissions to the IAM Role

Select the role you just created and open the Permissions tab. Click Add permissions. Then select Create Inline Policy and select the JSON tab.

Replace the existing content with this policy:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "ListS3Bucket",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "s3:ListBucket",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::gitlab-s3-deployment-demo-bucket"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "UploadAndDeleteObjects",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:PutObject",
        "s3:DeleteObject"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::gitlab-s3-deployment-demo-bucket/*" 
    }
  ]
}

Note: Replace the bucket name in the 

Resource
ARN above with your own S3 bucket name. The bucket name used in this tutorial is for demonstration purposes.

Then click Next. Enter the policy name and click Create policy.

So what do these permissions mean?

PermissionPurpose
s3:ListBucket
 Allows GitLab to list objects in the bucket.
s3:PutObject
 Allows GitLab to upload files to the bucket.
s3:DeleteObject
 Allows GitLab to delete objects when synchronizing files with the 
--delete
option.

Step 8: Configure GitLab CI/CD Variables

Now that you've created your IAM role and attached the required S3 permissions, let's move to GitLab.

You need to provide GitLab with the IAM Role ARN so that your CI/CD pipeline can use it to authenticate with AWS through OIDC.

To do this, open your GitLab repository and, from the left navigation panel, click Settings. Select CI/CD.

Expand the Variables section and click Add variable.

Step 9: Create the GitLab CI/CD Pipeline

Now that you've configured GitLab CI/CD variables and created your IAM role, it's time to create the pipeline that automates deployment to Amazon S3.

GitLab uses a file called 

.gitlab-ci.yml
to define the jobs and instructions that should run whenever changes are pushed to the repository.

For this tutorial, your pipeline will:

  • Authenticate with AWS using OIDC.
  • Obtain temporary AWS credentials.
  • Upload our website files to the S3 bucket.
  • Synchronise changes whenever we push new updates.

Here's an example repository:

Ijaylab/practice-action-aws

Click the + icon to create a new file, or go to the Policy editor and your CI/CD code. Name the file 

.gitlab-ci.yml
and add the following configuration:
deploy_to_s3:
  stage: deploy

  image: ubuntu:latest

  id_tokens:
    GITLAB_OIDC_TOKEN:
      aud: sts.amazonaws.com

  before_script:
    - apt-get update
    - apt-get install -y curl unzip jq
    - curl "https://awscli.amazonaws.com/awscli-exe-linux-x86_64.zip" -o "awscliv2.zip"
    - unzip awscliv2.zip
    - ./aws/install

  script:
    - export AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE="/tmp/web-identity-token"
    - echo "$GITLAB_OIDC_TOKEN" > "$AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE"
    - export AWS_ROLE_SESSION_NAME="GitLab-OIDC-Session"
    - export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="us-east-1"
    - echo "$GITLAB_OIDC_TOKEN" | cut -d '.' -f2 | tr '_-' '/+' | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | jq '{sub, aud}'
    - aws sts get-caller-identity
    - aws s3 sync . s3://gitlab-s3-deployment-demo-bucket --delete --exclude ".git/*" --exclude ".gitlab-ci.yml"

  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'

So what's going on in this configuration?

  • deploy_to_s3: Names the job.
  • stage: Defines the deployment stage.
  • image: Provides the Ubuntu environment.
  • id_tokens: Requests an OIDC token.
  • before_script: Installs AWS CLI and other tools.
  • script: Runs the deployment commands.
  • AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE: Stores the OIDC token.
  • AWS_DEFAULT_REGION: Sets the AWS region.
  • aws sts get-caller-identity: Checks AWS authentication.
  • aws s3 sync: Uploads files to S3.
  • --delete: Removes outdated files.
  • --exclude: Skips files we don't need.
  • rules: Runs the job only on the main branch.

Important: Replace 

YOUR_AWS_REGION
with the actual region where you created your S3 bucket, for example 
eu-west-1
if that is your bucket's region.

This will trigger the GitLab pipeline.

Step 10: Verify the Deployment on Amazon S3

Now that your GitLab pipeline has successfully authenticated with AWS, the next step is to confirm that your website files have been uploaded to your S3 bucket.

To do that, open the AWS Management Console and go to Amazon S3, then Buckets. Open your bucket: gitlab-s3-deployment-demo-bucket.

Then click the Objects tab, and check that your website files are there:

  • index.html
  • error.html
  • style.css

These are the files that we created and uploaded to GitLab earlier.

Then go to the Properties tab of your S3 bucket. Scroll down to Static website hosting, and copy the Bucket website endpoint. Then paste it into your browser. Your website should load.

Step 11: Re-Testing Deployment

To confirm that automation works, open index.html in your repository and make a small change to the index page.

Then go back to the AWS console and refresh your S3 website hosting endpoint. You should see your updated website without manually uploading the file to S3.

That's the automation we wanted to achieve. GitLab handles the deployment whenever you push changes to your repository.

Step 12: Test the Error Page

Since you created an error.html file, let's confirm that it works on your S3 website.

Open your S3 bucket in the AWS Console and go to Properties. Then scroll down to Static website hosting and confirm that the Error document is set to error.html.

Next, copy your bucket website endpoint and open the endpoint in your browser and add a page that doesn't exist.

You should see the custom error page you created.

Once you've confirmed that both your homepage and error page work, you can proceed to cleanup.

Step 11: Clean Up Your AWS Resources

Since this is a learning project, you may want to remove the resources when you're done to avoid unnecessary AWS charges.

To do that, empty your S3 bucket and delete it if you no longer need it (AWS will charge). You can also delete the IAM role if you no longer need it (optional, as AWS doesn't charge). Finally, delete the IAM identity provider if no other project uses it (optional, as AWS doesn't charge).

Conclusion

That’s it! You now have GitLab deploying your website files to Amazon S3 for you.

You no longer have to log in to AWS and upload your files by hand every time you make a change. Now you just push your changes to GitLab, and the pipeline does the upload. And because we used OIDC, you didn't have to save any AWS keys anywhere.

I hope this tutorial helped you set up your own pipeline. If you ran into an error, check the job log. That is how I found my own mistakes while writing this.

Further Reading:

If you found this article helpful, feel free to share it.

I also build tools for people in tech. One of my recent projects is SubmitReady, which helps people prepare their AWS Community Builders applications. Whether you are a developer, technical writer, developer advocate, community manager, or work in another area of tech, you can use it to review your application and identify where you can make improvements.

If you prefer learning through videos, I also explain cloud and DevOps topics in simple terms on my YouTube channel.

You can also follow me on Twitter, LinkedIn and GitHub.

Thank you for reading!

entries.content:
If you've created a Next.js project with shadcn/ui recently, there's a good chance dark mode is already set up.

I noticed this while looking through a fresh project. I opened 

app/globals.css
expecting to add the theme colors, but the light and dark values were already there. Then I checked the 
components
folder and found a 
theme-provider.tsx
file that had already been created for me.

That raised a more useful question: if shadcn has already done most of the setup, what do you actually need to build?

In this guide, we'll look at the dark-mode setup that comes with a generated shadcn project, understand how the pieces work together, and build a theme switcher that users can control. We'll also look at how to customize the colors without adding light and dark classes to every component.

By the end, you'll know:

  • Where shadcn stores its light and dark theme values
  • How CSS variables and Tailwind theme variables work together
  • What 
    next-themes
    does in a Next.js project
  • How to add a two-state or three-option theme switcher
  • How to add your own theme tokens

We'll start with the generated project and work through the theme setup before building the switcher.

Before you start: This guide follows the Next.js project generated by shadcn/create. Your project may look a little different if you use another framework, an older shadcn setup, or a different component style. I'll point out the parts you should check in your own project.

The examples and screenshots in this article are based on the companion project. Once you have the project locally, you can run 

pnpm install
and 
pnpm dev
to try it yourself.

The same page is shown in both themes. Only the active theme values change.

The page uses the same JSX in both screenshots. The theme changes the values behind the CSS variables, and the browser updates the styles.

Table of Contents

Project Setup and Versions

The versions below are the versions used in the companion project, which was generated in August 2026. Shadcn's generated output changes over time, so check your own

1. Create a shadcn Project

You don't need to configure Next.js and Tailwind from scratch for this guide. Shadcn's project builder can generate a starter project with the theme setup included.

Open shadcn/create and select Get Started.

Choose the style, base color, chart color, fonts, icon library, and radius from the controls. These choices affect the theme values that will be added to your project. We'll look at those values in the next section.

When you're happy with the setup, select Get Code, choose Next.js, and copy the command.

Run the command in your terminal. The preset ID in your command may be different from the example below:

pnpm dlx shadcn@latest init --preset b0 --template next

If you're building a complete product, you may prefer to start with a ready-made shadcn template and adapt it to your app. The same theme setup covered in this guide can be used in a template-based project.

│   ├── layout.tsx           # fonts and ThemeProvider already wired

Open 

http://localhost:3000

d
switches between light and dark mode.

The important point is that the theme setup is already present. Before adding anything, let's see what the generator has configured.

A generated project includes most of the pieces you need for light and dark themes. Here's where to find them:

So the main piece you'll usually need to add is the control that lets someone choose a theme. The rest is already configured, although it's worth understanding before you start customizing it.

3. Where the Theme Colors Live

Open 

app/globals.css
. You'll find two groups of CSS variables: one inside 
:root
and another inside 
.dark
.

Here's a shortened example based on the generated project:

:root {
  --background: oklch(1 0 0);
  --foreground: oklch(0.147 0.004 49.25);
  --card: oklch(1 0 0);
  --card-foreground: oklch(0.147 0.004 49.25);
  --primary: oklch(0.555 0.163 48.998);
  --primary-foreground: oklch(0.987 0.022 95.277);
  --muted: oklch(0.97 0.001 106.424);
  --muted-foreground: oklch(0.553 0.013 58.071);
  --border: oklch(0.923 0.003 48.717);
  --radius: 0.625rem;
  /* …about thirty in total */
}

.dark {
  --background: oklch(0.147 0.004 49.25);
  --foreground: oklch(0.985 0.001 106.423);
  --card: oklch(0.216 0.006 56.043);
  --card-foreground: oklch(0.985 0.001 106.423);
  --primary: oklch(0.473 0.137 46.201);
  --primary-foreground: oklch(0.987 0.022 95.277);
  --muted: oklch(0.268 0.007 34.298);
  --muted-foreground: oklch(0.709 0.01 56.259);
  --border: oklch(1 0 0 / 10%);
}

The idea is straightforward:

:root   →  light theme values
.dark   →  dark theme values

Both blocks use the same variable names. The values change depending on whether the 

dark
class is present on the page.

For example, 

--background
is white in the light theme and near-black in the dark theme. 
--foreground
changes in the opposite direction so the text remains visible against the background.

You'll also see variables such as 

--radius
. It isn't a color, but it's part of the theme configuration. In this setup, the radius is defined once because the corner shape doesn't need a separate value for dark mode.

Why Semantic Tokens Are Useful

Theme variables are especially useful when you're building components. Compare these two examples.

Without semantic tokens, you might add separate light and dark colors directly to the component:


  Hello

That works, but you have to repeat the same decisions throughout your app. If your color palette changes, you'll need to find and update all those classes.

With semantic tokens, the component can use the theme variable instead:


  Hello

The component doesn't need to know whether the page is in light or dark mode. It uses 

background
and 
foreground
, and the active theme supplies the right values.

This is also why shadcn components such as 

Card
can adapt without needing dark-mode classes of their own:

  
    Hello

If you open 

components/ui/card.tsx
, you'll see classes such as 
bg-card
and 
text-card-foreground
. The component uses the semantic tokens, while the theme defines what those tokens look like.

The same idea applies when you add more UI to the project. If you need examples of individual elements built for the shadcn ecosystem, you can refer to Shadcn Components and adapt the ones that fit your interface. Keep the semantic tokens in place so those components follow your light and dark themes.

Understanding the Foreground Pairs

Many theme tokens come in pairs. The first token describes a surface, and the 

-foreground
token describes the text or content that appears on top of it.
Surface tokenForeground token
--background
 
--foreground
 
--card
 
--card-foreground
 
--primary
 
--primary-foreground
 
--muted
 
--muted-foreground

For example, 

bg-primary text-primary-foreground
uses a matching background and text color. The theme defines both values together so the combination works across its light and dark palettes.

Some tokens, such as 

--border
, 
--input
, and 
--ring
, don't need a foreground pair because they're used for borders, input outlines, and focus indicators.

The companion project displays the token pairs as simple tiles. Each tile uses the same 

bg- text--foreground
pattern.

The markup stays the same in both screenshots. Only the active CSS variable values change. The demo also includes a custom 

--warning
token to show how you can extend the theme.

4. How Tailwind Gets its Theme Classes

There's one more part of 

globals.css
that's easy to overlook: the 
@theme inline
block.

A CSS variable such as 

--primary
is available to CSS, but defining it doesn't automatically create Tailwind classes such as 
bg-primary
or 
text-primary
. Tailwind needs to know which variables should become utility classes.

That's what this block does:

@theme inline {
  --color-background: var(--background);
  --color-foreground: var(--foreground);
  --color-primary: var(--primary);
  --color-primary-foreground: var(--primary-foreground);
  --color-muted: var(--muted);
  /* …one line per token */
  --radius-sm: calc(var(--radius) * 0.6);
  --radius-md: calc(var(--radius) * 0.8);
  --radius-lg: var(--radius);
  --radius-xl: calc(var(--radius) * 1.4);
}

For example, this line:

--color-primary: var(--primary);

connects the CSS variable 

--primary
to Tailwind's color utilities. It allows you to use classes such as 
bg-primary
, 
text-primary
, and 
border-primary
.

This is an important step when you add your own tokens. If you define 

--brand
in 
:root
but don't add a matching 
--color-brand
entry in 
@theme inline
, Tailwind won't generate the 
bg-brand
utility for you. The CSS variable can exist and still not be available as a Tailwind utility.

The 

inline
keyword is also important here. It allows the generated utilities to reference the underlying CSS variable, so they use the current value when the theme changes.

What the 
dark:
Variant Does

You'll also find this line in 

globals.css
:
@custom-variant dark (&:is(.dark *));

This defines how Tailwind's 

dark:
variant works in this setup. A class such as 
dark:hidden
applies when the element is inside an ancestor with the 
dark
class.

There are two details to remember:

  • The theme is represented by a 
    dark
    class, rather than a 
    data-theme
    attribute.
  • The selector targets descendants of the element with the 
    dark
    class.

In this project, 

next-themes
adds the class to the 
 element. That means the elements inside the page can use 
dark:
 utilities as expected.
Here's the relationship between the theme class, CSS variables, and Tailwind utilities:
.dark on 
   ↓
--primary changes value          (globals.css)
   ↓
--color-primary reads it         (@theme inline)
   ↓
bg-primary compiles to var(--primary)
   ↓
every element using bg-primary repaints



When the theme changes, the browser updates the CSS variables and recalculates the styles that use them. Your components don't need to re-render just because a theme color changed.
So far, we've looked at the CSS side. The next question is what adds or removes the 
dark
 class.
5. What 
next-themes
 Does


CSS defines what the light and dark themes look like. It doesn't remember a visitor's choice or decide which theme should be active. That's handled by JavaScript.
The generated Next.js project uses 
next-themes
 for this.
The library handles a few things for you:
  • Adds or removes the 
    dark
     class on the 
     element.
  • Saves the selected theme in 
    localStorage
    .
  • Supports a 
    system
     option that follows the visitor's operating system preference.
  • Runs a small script before the page is displayed so the saved theme can be applied early.
That last point helps prevent a flash of the wrong theme when the page loads. If you wait until a React 
useEffect
 runs to apply the theme, the browser may display the page before the effect runs. A visitor who prefers dark mode could briefly see the light version first.
The generated project already includes a theme provider and mounts it in the app layout. Let's take a look at what it does.
6. The Theme Provider That's Already in Your Project
The generated 
components/theme-provider.tsx
 file wraps 
next-themes
 and sets a few defaults. Here's the provider from the companion project:
"use client"

import * as React from "react"
import { ThemeProvider as NextThemesProvider, useTheme } from "next-themes"

function ThemeProvider({
  children,
  ...props
}: React.ComponentProps) {
  return (

  )
}



The wrapper means you don't need to repeat the same configuration every time you use the provider. In 
app/layout.tsx
, it can be mounted like this:
{children}



The 
{...props}
 spread comes after the default props. That means a value passed to 
ThemeProvider
 can override the wrapper's defaults.
There's a Keyboard Shortcut Too
The provider file also includes a 
ThemeHotkey
 component:
function isTypingTarget(target: EventTarget | null) {
  if (!(target instanceof HTMLElement)) {
    return false
  }

  return (
    target.isContentEditable ||
    target.tagName === "INPUT" ||
    target.tagName === "TEXTAREA" ||
    target.tagName === "SELECT"
  )
}

function ThemeHotkey() {
  const { resolvedTheme, setTheme } = useTheme()

  React.useEffect(() => {
    function onKeyDown(event: KeyboardEvent) {
      if (event.defaultPrevented || event.repeat) return
      if (event.metaKey || event.ctrlKey || event.altKey) return
      if (event.key.toLowerCase() !== "d") return
      if (isTypingTarget(event.target)) return

      setTheme(resolvedTheme === "dark" ? "light" : "dark")
    }

    window.addEventListener("keydown", onKeyDown)
    return () => window.removeEventListener("keydown", onKeyDown)
  }, [resolvedTheme, setTheme])

  return null
}



This component doesn't render anything on the page. It listens for the 
d
 key and switches between light and dark mode.
Notice the checks inside the keyboard handler. They prevent the shortcut from firing when the user is typing in an input, textarea, select, or editable element. The modifier-key check also prevents the shortcut from interfering with combinations such as 
Cmd+D
 or 
Ctrl+D
.
If you don't want this shortcut in your project, remove

attribute="class"

.dark
, so 
next-themes

data-theme

If your switcher uses animated icons, this setting can affect their transitions. The behavior is worth considering when you decide how theme changes should look across the page.
Why

The theme script can update the

suppressHydrationWarning

7. Build a Theme Switcher
At this point, the theme colors are configured and 
next-themes

There are two common approaches. You can give users a button that switches between light and dark, or offer a menu with Light, Dark, and System options.
Option 1: A light and Dark Toggle
If your app only needs two modes, a single button is enough:

First, use

"system"
, while

Second, keep both icons in the DOM. The 
Sun

Moon

For comparison, this conditional approach can cause a mismatch between the server-rendered markup and the browser's first render:

Finally, add an accessible label. Since the button only contains an icon, 
aria-label

Option 2: A Light, Dark, and System Menu
If you want users to choose their preferred mode, including the operating system setting, use a dropdown menu.
First, add the dropdown menu component if it's not already in your project:
pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add dropdown-menu



Then create the switcher:

import { useTheme } from "next-themes"

The menu uses a radio group so the current option is shown as selected. This makes it easier for users to see whether Light, Dark, or System is active.
There are two implementation details to pay attention to here.
First, base UI uses 
render
 instead of 
asChild
. The companion project uses the 
base-nova
 style, which is built on Base UI. In this setup, the dropdown trigger uses the 
render
 prop to render the shadcn button. Many older examples use 
asChild
, which is common in Radix-based projects. Check your own 
components.json
 and component imports before copying an example.
Use a radio group for mutually exclusive options. Light, Dark, and System are three choices where only one can be active at a time. 
DropdownMenuRadioGroup
 communicates that relationship and displays the selected option.
The expression 
theme ?? "system"
 uses 
"system"
 as a fallback if the theme value is still undefined. This keeps the radio group controlled while 
next-themes

You may have seen the 
next-themes

theme
. That advice is for UI the server renders. Here, the radio items only appear when someone opens the menu, which always happens after the page has hydrated, so the server never renders a theme value and there's nothing to mismatch.
You can now place the switcher in your header or another part of your layout. For example:
import { ModeToggle } from "@/components/mode-toggle"



  
My app

  





Choose one switcher for your app, based on how much control you want to give users. You don't need to display both versions at once.
The switcher will usually sit inside a larger page, such as an account settings screen or dashboard. If you're building that kind of page, shadcn blocks can give you useful layout examples. You can adapt a block to your needs and keep using the same theme tokens for its backgrounds, borders, and text.
8. Why the Icon Animation May Not Work
You might want the sun and moon icons to rotate or scale when someone changes the theme. The shadcn examples include transition classes like these:





But the generated provider also uses 
disableTransitionOnChange
. This option temporarily injects a stylesheet that disables transitions while the theme is changing. The rule used by the installed 
next-themes
 version is:
*,*::before,*::after{transition:none!important}



Because the rule uses 
!important
, it can override the 
transition-transform
 classes on the icons during the theme change. The icons may switch immediately instead of animating.
There's a reason this option exists. Without it, every element with a CSS transition may animate its colors when the theme changes. Depending on your design, that can make the entire page feel slow or distracting.
You have a few options:
  • Keep 
    disableTransitionOnChange
     and use icons without transition effects.
  • Remove the option if you want the page and icons to transition together.
  • Keep the option and use a CSS animation or a motion library for the icon effect. Test this with your actual setup to make sure the animation behaves as expected.
The important thing is to understand that the provider setting affects more than the theme colors. It can also affect transitions elsewhere in your interface.
9. Customize Your Theme
Once you understand where the theme values live, changing your app's colors becomes much easier. You can update a token once and have every component that uses it pick up the new value.
Change an Existing Token
Imagine your brand uses blue as its primary color. You could set a blue background directly on one button:




But this only changes that button. If you want the primary color to be consistent across your app, update the 
--primary
 token in 
app/globals.css
 instead:
:root {
  --primary: oklch(0.55 0.18 265);
  --primary-foreground: oklch(0.99 0 0);
}

.dark {
  --primary: oklch(0.62 0.16 265);
  --primary-foreground: oklch(0.17 0.02 265);
}



The same token is used by components and utilities throughout the project. Update both the 
:root
 and 
.dark
 values so the color works in both themes.
The two values don't have to be identical. A color that looks good on a light background may need a different lightness or saturation on a dark background. The generated theme uses different values for some tokens for exactly this reason.
The project also uses 
oklch()
 color values. In this color format, the first value represents lightness, which can make it easier to adjust how bright or dark a color appears while keeping its hue consistent.
You can customize the border radius in the same way. The generated 
@theme inline
 block derives several radius utilities from the 
--radius
 value, so changing it updates the overall corner scale:
--radius: 0.625rem;



Add a Custom Token
You can also add tokens that aren't included in the default theme. For example, let's add a 
warning
 color that can be used for a notice or alert.
First, define the token and its foreground color in both theme blocks. Then connect those variables to Tailwind in 
@theme inline
:
:root {
  --warning: oklch(0.84 0.16 84);
  --warning-foreground: oklch(0.28 0.07 46);
}

.dark {
  --warning: oklch(0.41 0.11 46);
  --warning-foreground: oklch(0.99 0.02 95);
}

@theme inline {
  --color-warning: var(--warning);
  --color-warning-foreground: var(--warning-foreground);
}



You can now use the new classes in a component:

  Your trial ends in 3 days.





The component uses the same classes in both screenshots. The theme supplies the appropriate background and text colors.
Remember to add the 
--color-warning
 and 
--color-warning-foreground
 entries to 
@theme inline
. Without those entries, the CSS variables will exist, but Tailwind won't generate the corresponding utility classes.
It's also a good idea to define a foreground token whenever you add a new surface color. That way, the background and text colors are designed to work together.
When Should You Use 
dark:


Once your theme uses semantic tokens, you won't need 
dark:
 classes for most background and text colors.
For example, instead of maintaining separate light and dark background classes:
// You're now maintaining this color in two places



// The token already knows





Use a semantic token such as 
bg-muted
 when it represents the color you want. The token already has values for both themes.
There are still cases where 
dark:
 is useful. You might need to swap an image, adjust a shadow, or change a decorative element that doesn't fit into your semantic color tokens. Use it when the appearance genuinely needs a theme-specific rule.
Conclusion
A generated shadcn project already includes most of the setup needed for light and dark mode. The part you usually need to build is the switcher that gives users control over the theme.
Here's a quick recap:
  1. :root
     and 
    .dark
     define the theme values. They use the same variable names with different values.
  2. @theme inline
     connects CSS variables to Tailwind utilities**.** Add a matching entry when you create a custom token.
  3. next-themes
     applies the active theme. In this setup, it adds or removes the 
    dark
     class on 
    .
  4. The generated project already includes the provider. Check 
    components/theme-provider.tsx
     and 
    app/layout.tsx
     before creating another one.
  5. The visible switcher is the part you add. Use a simple toggle or a menu with Light, Dark, and System options.
  6. Customize tokens instead of styling every component separately. This keeps your colors consistent across the app.
Once you know how these pieces fit together, dark mode becomes easier to maintain. You can update the theme in one place, add new tokens when you need them, and let your components use those values without having to check which theme is active.

  • shadcn theming: Theme tokens and CSS variables.
  • next-themes: Theme provider documentation and source.
  • Tailwind CSS theme variables: How theme variables create utility classes.
  • Base UI: Documentation for the primitives used by the 
    base-nova
     style.
  • MDN: 
    oklch()
    : Reference for the OKLCH color format.
Thanks for Reading
The companion project includes both switcher examples, the custom 
warning
 token, and the page used for the screenshots. To try the examples locally, clone the repository, then run 
pnpm install
 followed by 
pnpm dev
 from the project directory.
Companion GitHub repository:- https://github.com/shadcnstudio/shadcn-dark-mode-guide
If you try the examples and run into something that behaves differently in your setup, leave a comment with your shadcn style and package versions. That context makes it much easier to work out what's happening.

entries.content:
Phishing attacks are getting harder to recognize. And no, it isn't just because hackers have become better at hiding spelling mistakes. Some phishing emails now look almost identical to genuine security alerts, complete with familiar company logos, professional language, and links that take you to websites that look exactly like the real thing.

You might think you're logging into your GitHub account to fix a security issue, when you're actually giving your login details to someone else. That's not exactly the kind of account activity you want.

The interesting part is that attackers don't always need to find a weakness in an application's code. Sometimes, convincing a person to share their password is all it takes. This is where social engineering comes in, combining human behaviour with technical tricks to steal sensitive information.

In this article, we'll break down how phishing attacks actually work and look at the different techniques attackers use. We'll also understand how developers can spot suspicious URLs, inspect email authentication, and protect their applications from credential theft. Then we'll look at what happens behind a fake login page and why even that little HTTPS padlock isn't a guarantee that a website is safe.

What We'll Cover:

What Is a Phishing Attack and Why Does It Work?

Phishing is fundamentally a psychological exploit wrapped in a technological delivery system. Before looking at the code and infrastructure involved, you need to understand the human elements that make these attacks so consistently successful.

Phishing Is More About Human Behavior Than Hacking

At its core, phishing is a form of social engineering. Attackers impersonate trusted people, companies, or services to manipulate their targets. Their primary objective is usually to steal login credentials, harvest financial information or gain initial access to restricted systems.

Rather than searching for a vulnerability in a firewall, the attacker searches for a vulnerability in human judgment. They manufacture situations designed to bypass critical thinking, relying on specific emotional triggers to influence the victim's decisions.

Why People Fall for Phishing Messages

The science behind why intelligent people fall for these scams comes down to cognitive load and neurobiology. When a person reads a message demanding immediate action, the brain's amygdala, responsible for processing fear and urgency, often overrides the prefrontal cortex, which handles logical analysis.

Attackers weaponize this biological response using several common triggers. They create urgency by claiming an account will be suspended if the user doesn't act immediately. They leverage fear by suggesting someone has already compromised the victim's data. They project authority by spoofing emails from a manager or an IT administrator. Alternatively, they spark curiosity by vaguely mentioning the victim in a shared document.

Technical knowledge doesn't automatically make someone immune to this kind of psychological manipulation. The Verizon 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report consistently demonstrates that the human element, including social engineering and credential abuse, remains a primary catalyst in the vast majority of security breaches. When a developer is tired, distracted or managing a high cognitive load, a well-crafted fake alert can easily slip past their regular defenses.

How Phishing Attacks Actually Work: A Step-by-Step Breakdown

To truly understand the threat, developers need to see the lifecycle of an attack. Consider a fictional, yet highly realistic, phishing campaign targeting a developer's GitHub account.

Step 1: The Attacker Chooses a Target

Attackers rarely send emails completely at random when targeting high-value infrastructure. They actively identify potential victims by scraping public information. A developer with a public GitHub profile, an active LinkedIn presence, and a personal portfolio website is an ideal target.

The attacker compiles this publicly available data to understand what tools the developer uses, which repositories they contribute to, and what their primary email address is. This reconnaissance phase ensures the eventual payload is contextually relevant and highly believable.

Step 2: The Attacker Creates a Convincing Message

Using the gathered intelligence, the attacker crafts an email impersonating a trusted service. The developer receives an email claiming their GitHub account has been flagged for suspicious activity originating from an unknown IP address. To make the illusion complete, the attacker flawlessly imitates GitHub's branding, layout, typography, and terminology.

The email contains a prominent call-to-action button urging the developer to "Verify Account Activity." Because the message aligns with standard security alert protocols, the developer's initial suspicion is naturally lowered.

Step 3: The Victim Clicks a Fake Link

When the developer clicks the verification button, they're directed to a fraudulent website. This is where domain manipulation comes into play. The attacker will use lookalike domains, subtle misspellings, or misleading subdomains to disguise the destination.

For instance, the URL might read github.com.example-login.test. While the word "github" is present, the actual domain being accessed is example-login.test. Attackers also exploit URL redirects or utilize homograph attacks, where Cyrillic or unexpected Unicode characters replace standard Latin letters to create visually identical, yet fundamentally different, URLs.

Step 4: The Fake Website Collects Information

When they land on the fake website, the victim encounters a perfect clone of the legitimate login screen. When the developer enters their username and password, the browser doesn't send this data to GitHub's authentication servers. Instead, the fake login form executes a script that packages the credentials and transmits them directly to an attacker-controlled server.

According to comprehensive analysis in the Google Research paper Data Breaches, Phishing or Malware? Understanding the Risks of Stolen Credentials, stolen credentials are often tested or sold within hours, if not minutes, of being harvested.

Step 5: The Attacker Uses the Stolen Credentials

Once the attacker possesses the compromised credentials, the fallout is immediate. They use the stolen username and password to log into the real GitHub platform. From there, they can access private repositories, inject malicious code into production branches, or extract exposed API keys and environment secrets.

Also, because password reuse is incredibly common, the attacker will likely test these same credentials against the developer's email, cloud hosting provider and internal company portals, exponentially increasing the effect of a single mistaken click.

The Different Types of Phishing Attacks Developers Should Know

While the GitHub scenario illustrates a standard attack, threat actors utilize several variations depending on their goals and resources. Understanding these variations helps in identifying the specific vector being used.

Email Phishing

This is the traditional approach involving fake emails distributed to a large number of recipients. These campaigns cast a wide net, impersonating ubiquitous services like banks, package delivery companies, or software platforms, hoping a small percentage of recipients will engage with the malicious links.

Spear Phishing

Unlike mass email campaigns, spear phishing is a highly targeted attack designed for a specific individual or organization. Attackers leverage detailed information about a person's job role, current projects, colleagues, or preferred software tools to make the message incredibly believable.

A spear-phishing email might reference a specific Jira ticket or a recent deployment, making it nearly indistinguishable from legitimate internal communication.

Clone Phishing

In a clone phishing attack, the adversary intercepts or acquires a legitimate email that was previously delivered. They create an exact replica of this email but replace the original safe links or attachments with malicious ones. Because the recipient recognizes the context and the sender of the original conversation, they are highly likely to trust the cloned version.

Smishing and Vishing

Phishing isn't confined to the inbox. Smishing involves sending malicious links or urgent alerts through SMS text messages. Vishing relies on voice calls, where the attacker uses social engineering over the phone, often utilizing AI voice-cloning technology to extract passwords or multi-factor authentication codes directly from the victim.

Business Email Compromise (BEC)

BEC is a sophisticated financial attack where threat actors impersonate executives, managers, or vendors. The goal is rarely to steal a password. Instead, they trick employees into authorizing fraudulent wire transfers, modifying payroll details, or sharing sensitive corporate data.

The APWG Phishing Activity Trends Report routinely highlights BEC as one of the most financially devastating forms of social engineering targeting modern enterprises.

How Developers Can Spot a Phishing Attack

Moving beyond general security awareness, developers have the technical literacy to inspect the underlying mechanics of a suspicious message. Identifying phishing requires analyzing the structural components of web traffic and email protocols.

Inspect the URL Before Trusting the Website

The most reliable way to identify a fraudulent website is by dissecting its URL. Attackers rely on the fact that most users only glance at the address bar. Developers should look for lookalike domains, unexpected subdomains, and URL shorteners designed to hide the final destination.

It's crucial to identify the actual root domain serving the page. For example, https://github.com/login is the legitimate endpoint. In contrast, https://github-login.example.com and https://github.com.example.net/login both resolve to attacker-controlled domains, regardless of the presence of the word "github."

Studies analyzing automated detection systems, such as research on Evaluating the Robustness of Phishing Web Page Detection Models, emphasize that analyzing lexical features and domain registration anomalies remains one of the most effective ways to identify malicious infrastructure.

Check the Email Headers and Sender Information

Display names in email clients are easily forged, but email headers reveal the actual routing path. Developers should inspect the From, Reply-To, and Return-Path addresses for discrepancies.

More importantly, checking the authentication headers provides important insight. SPF (Sender Policy Framework) verifies that the sending server is authorized by the domain owner. DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) uses cryptographic signatures to ensure the email content has not been altered in transit. DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) ties SPF and DKIM together, dictating how receivers should handle emails that fail these checks.

While passing these checks doesn't guarantee absolute safety, failing them is a massive red flag.

Look for Suspicious Login Behavior

Context is just as important as the technical indicators. Developers should constantly question unexpected authentication prompts.

If you receive a password reset notification you didn't request or a multi-factor authentication (MFA) approval prompt for a session you didn't initiate, an attacker is likely testing your credentials.

Similarly, any service demanding that you manually share API keys, session tokens, or passwords through a chat interface or email should be immediately classified as hostile.

Examine Links and Attachments Carefully

Malicious payloads are frequently hidden within attachments. Unexpected executable files are obvious threats, but unusual document attachments, such as PDFs or Office files containing embedded macros, are equally dangerous. Links should always match the contextual premise of the message.

It's important to emphasize that spelling mistakes and grammatical errors are no longer a reliable metric for identifying phishing. With the advent of generative AI, modern phishing emails are often impeccably written and flawlessly formatted.

A Developer's Perspective: What Happens Behind a Phishing Login Page?

To fully grasp the danger, it helps to look at the attack from an architectural perspective. The difference between a legitimate authentication flow and a credential harvesting operation comes down to data destination.

Understanding a Normal Login Request

When a user logs into a legitimate modern web application, the frontend collects the input and transmits it via an asynchronous HTTP request. A simplified example looks like this:

async function login(email, password) {
  const response = await fetch("/api/login", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json"
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      email,
      password
    })
  });

  return response.json();
}

In this legitimate flow, the browser sends the POST request to the official backend API. The server validates the credentials against a securely hashed database entry, generates a session token or cookie, and responds with an authentication success result.

What Makes a Phishing Login Page Different?

A phishing page entirely bypasses this established backend. While the HTML and CSS create a familiar visual interface, the underlying JavaScript is fundamentally different. Instead of sending the payload to /api/login on the official domain, the script submits the entered information to an external, attacker-controlled endpoint. The user interacts with the fake interface and the POST request quietly ships their plaintext credentials to a remote database.

After the data is stolen, the script typically redirects the victim to the real website's legitimate login page, leaving them confused but unaware that a theft just occurred.

Why HTTPS Does Not Make a Phishing Website Safe

There's a persistent misconception that the padlock icon in the browser address bar signifies that a website is trustworthy. This is technologically false. HTTPS simply means the communication channel between the browser and the web server is secure. Just because a website uses encryption, much like how an encrypted email like Proton Mail protects your personal messages from outside snooping during transit, it doesn't verify the actual identity of the person operating the server on the other end.

Attackers can easily and freely obtain valid TLS certificates for their malicious domains. Ultimately, a phishing site equipped with HTTPS simply ensures that your credentials are stolen securely, preventing third-party eavesdroppers on the network from intercepting the data before the phisher receives it.

How Developers Can Protect Their Applications From Phishing Attacks

Identifying phishing as an end-user is only half the battle. Developers are uniquely positioned to architect systems that mitigate the impact of phishing attacks against their own user base.

Implement Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)

Passwords alone are an insufficient defense against credential harvesting. Implementing MFA adds a distinct verification layer.

But not all MFA is created equal. SMS-based codes can be intercepted and simple push notifications are vulnerable to "MFA fatigue" attacks, where adversaries spam the user until they accidentally approve a request.

Developers should prioritize phishing-resistant authentication methods, such as hardware security keys (like YubiKeys) or WebAuthn/Passkey implementations, which cryptographically bind the authentication attempt to the legitimate domain, making stolen passwords useless.

Use Secure Authentication Practices

Application security fundamentally requires robust backend practices. Passwords must never be stored in plain text they must be hashed using strong, salted algorithms like bcrypt or Argon2.

Developers should implement aggressive rate limiting on login endpoints to prevent credential stuffing attacks using previously phished password lists. Also, session management should be ironclad, utilizing HttpOnly and Secure flags on cookies to prevent cross-site scripting (XSS) from exposing authentication tokens.

Validate Redirects and External URLs

Improperly configured redirect mechanisms often inadvertently assist phishing campaigns. If a web application uses unvalidated input to determine where to send a user after login (an "open redirect" vulnerability), attackers can craft a link to the legitimate site that automatically forwards the user to a malicious clone.

Developers should strictly validate redirect destinations against an internal allowlist, especially during authentication and password reset workflows.

Configure Email Authentication

To prevent attackers from easily spoofing the application's official email domain, developers and operations teams should configure DNS-based email authentication. Implementing SPF, DKIM, and DMARC creates a verifiable chain of trust.

As outlined in the NIST Phishing Guidance, these protocols are essential for reducing domain spoofing. While they won't stop an attacker from registering a lookalike domain, they will stop them from sending emails that appear to originate exactly from your actual company servers.

What Should You Do If You Accidentally Click a Phishing Link?

Even the most vigilant developers can make a mistake during a stressful deployment or a chaotic workday. Knowing what your incident response plan is and how to execute it right away is crucial for containment.

If You Only Clicked the Link

If you click a suspicious link but immediately recognize the threat before entering any data, close the browser tab immediately. Don't interact with the page, avoid downloading any files, and certainly don't accept any browser permission requests.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security notes that simply clicking a link doesn't automatically mean your machine is infected, provided your browser and operating system are fully updated. But if a file automatically downloaded or executed, you should disconnect from the network and follow your organization's formal incident response procedure.

If You Entered Your Credentials

If you typed your password and hit submit, assume the credentials are compromised instantly. Navigate directly to the official website by typing the URL yourself and change your password immediately.

If the application allows it, manually revoke all active sessions. Review your recent login history for unrecognized IP addresses. If you haven't already, enable a phishing-resistant MFA method. And if you reused that exact password on any other service, you'll need change it on those platforms as well.

Report the Phishing Attempt

Reporting is a critical community defense mechanism. Notify your internal security or IT team immediately so they can investigate the domain, block the malicious IP addresses at the firewall, and alert other employees who may have received the same message. Ignoring the mistake only gives the attacker more time to exploit the access they just gained.

Final Thoughts

Phishing is a reminder that breaking into an account doesn't always require breaking into its code. Sometimes, all it takes is a convincing email, a familiar-looking login page, and a moment when someone isn't paying enough attention.

That's what makes these attacks interesting from a security perspective. They target both the technology we build and the people who use it. Developers can make authentication stronger, protect sensitive data, and close security gaps, but they also need to understand how attackers exploit human behaviour. Because at the end of the day, a secure application keeps hackers out and also doesn't make things easy for them when someone accidentally lets them in.

entries.content:
The Microsoft Azure AI Fundamentals (AI-901) is an entry-level certification that covers AI concepts, Microsoft Foundry, and a set of Azure AI services. It replaces the AI-900, and its exam guide is organized into just two domains.

We just published a course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel that will help you prepare for and pass the AI-901 exam. This course is taught by Andrew Brown of ExamPro.

The course combines lectures with hands-on labs that you complete in your own Azure account. You will need some knowledge of Python syntax, and Andrew recommends taking Azure Fundamentals first, since this course does not cover basic Azure knowledge.

In this course, you will learn:

  • Machine Learning & AI Concepts

    How datasets, labeling, features, regression, classification, clustering, and neural networks fit into a simple ML pipeline.
  • Generative AI Foundations

    How large language models work, including transformer architecture, tokenization, embeddings, positional encoding, and attention.
  • Responsible AI

    The principles of fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, and accountability, along with Microsoft's Responsible AI Standard V2.
  • Microsoft Foundry & Azure AI Services

    How to compare and deploy models from the Foundry model catalog and work with Azure Speech, Azure Language, OCR, and Content Understanding.
  • Prompt Engineering & Model Testing

    How system prompts, zero-shot and few-shot prompting, chaining, and chain of thought work in the Foundry playground, plus how model pricing is calculated.
  • Foundry Applications & Agents

    How to use the Microsoft Foundry SDK to connect to a deployed model, control tool calls, and create a Foundry agent.

Watch the full course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel (4.5-hour watch).
